1:
Everything turns on who is spoken of. John Gill says the calling of the Gentiles is not to be doubted here, since Paul quoted and applied it so, describing those who asked not as people without Christ and without the promises, in no expectation of his coming. John Wesley is equally firm, adding that the point cannot be doubted by any who will not arrogate to themselves a greater ability to interpret the older prophecies than Paul had; the word rendered sought, he notes, signifies diligent enquiry in things relating to God. Matthew Henry calls Paul an expositor we may depend upon, and notes how bold the prophet is in foretelling it to a people who would take it as an affront. He draws the doctrine from the order of events: God anticipates their prayers with his blessings, so that they came to know him because they were known of him. In after-communion, Henry allows, God is found of those that seek him; but in first conversion he is found of those that seek him not, for we love him because he first loved us.

Charles Ellicott dissents on both counts. He doubts first that these words answer the prayer closing the previous chapter, since the sequence is not continuous, and thinks it likelier they were written after an interval, explaining why that appeal met no immediate answer. He doubts second that the Gentiles are in view at all. Taking the text as it stands, and there being no reference to the Gentiles afterwards, he judges the same people to be addressed throughout, both verses speaking of indifference and hardness, so that the sense is: I was ready to answer those who did not enquire, was nigh to be discovered by those who did not seek. He prefers too the rendering a nation that has not called on my name, the meaning either way being that Israel had sunk to the level of the heathen. Keil and Delitzsch weigh the question more evenly. They grant that the apostle depended here on the Greek translation, which was in his own hands and his readers’, and which naturally suggests the allusion to the Gentiles. Three things throw weight into that scale: the interchange of the two words for nation and people, the attribute not called by my name, which applies to heathen only, and the harmony with the context if God contrasts his success among the Gentiles with his failure in Israel. Nevertheless, they conclude, these are not decisive if we look at the Hebrew alone.

Adam Clarke works at the wording, following the Greek and the apostle in rendering the clause I am made known to those that asked not for me, but reports that the verb strictly means I am sought so as to be found, which leaves the next verb without its object; some render the whole I have answered those that asked not, as the ancient versions do elsewhere. He leaves the choice to the reader. On the spreading of the hands the voices converge again. Gill has God inviting them daily by every method while they remained inflexible, the gospel being preached to them first until the apostles turned away. Henry makes the gesture argue: not a beckoning with the finger but hands spread as one reasoning and expostulating, ready to embrace, and spread all the day, all the gospel day, so that even those who came at the eleventh hour were not rejected. Wesley hears the hands of a passionate orator persuading and of a liberal benefactor loading them with benefits. Ellicott grants that here the words were meant for Israel—then notes that they stand over the portal of a church at the entrance of the Ghetto at Rome, and turns the reproach round: of how many churches might it not be said, thou art the man, the beam is in thine own eye.
3:
The charge is provocation done openly. John Gill notes that these sins were committed without fear of the divine Being, in the open streets and even in the place of the divine residence, and committed constantly; John Wesley calls it the utmost impudence, taking no notice of God’s omnipresence. Adam Clarke reads the particulars as heathen practices to which the people were immoderately addicted before the captivity. The heathen worshipped in groves, and against that the law had commanded that the places where the Canaanites served their gods be destroyed and their groves burnt; and where the altar was to be of unhewn stone, these built of brick. Clarke offers an alternative: the phrase may mean they sacrificed on the flat roofs of their houses, as with the altars on an upper chamber which a reforming king beat down. Charles Ellicott also prefers the roofs, and observes that sacrificing in gardens was common in Judah under Ahaz, which bears on the chapter’s date; he mentions, with less probability, brick altars used by the exiles.

The graves and monuments raise the question of necromancy. Gill says they remained among the graves to consult the dead, where they imagined spirits haunted and fancied they might get knowledge of things to come; Wesley agrees, and reports the monuments taken both of idol temples and of caves where the heathen worshipped. Clarke cites the opinion that they lodged in desert places so that demons might appear to them, and notes that the word rendered monuments is doubtful, some manuscripts reading in the rocks, the Greek in the caves. He supplies a modern parallel: among the Highlanders a man was wrapped in the hide of a newly slain bullock and left in some wild spot where the scenery suggested nothing but horror, and whatever his exalted imagination impressed on him there passed for the inspiration of the spirits that haunt such places. Ellicott is more cautious: the rock graves, though ceremonially unclean, were often used as dwellings, so the charge may be merely one of neglecting the law; but it may imply necromancy, and he recalls that men slept in the crypts of a healing god’s temple in hope of visions.

On the unclean food both textual and historical points arise. Clarke notes that swine’s flesh was forbidden by the law but in principal request among the heathen for their sacrifices, so that a persecutor could use it as the test of apostasy, and that the broth of abominable meats served for lustrations and magical arts. Ellicott argues the prohibition rested not on sanitary grounds but on the animal’s place in the festivals of Thammuz, and turns the point against those who date the chapter among the exiles: no swine is mentioned in the cuneiform inscriptions, whereas in Egypt as in Palestine it was reckoned unclean. The broth he takes for a sacrificial feast of unclean meats, perhaps joined to divination from the viscera. The last verse gives the sting. Gill reports the reading by which these are the unclean persons themselves, telling the righteous to keep to their own company. Ellicott finds the picture reminiscent of the proud exclusiveness of the later Pharisees, the root evil identical, but marks the difference: the ground here is not any consciousness of Israel’s privileges but an actual apostasy, the speakers boasting of initiation into heathen mysteries as a consecrated character setting them above the Israelites who kept faith with the God of their fathers. He renders the phrase literally, I am holy to thee, one whom thou mayest not approach, and rejects as less satisfactory the transitive reading that makes it a claim to impart holiness; and he notes that the punishment is not put in the future, the self-exalting idolaters being already as men consumed in the fire of divine wrath. Wesley says their whole holiness lay in rituals, and those such as God never commanded.
6:
The record is the point of the first verse. John Gill takes the writing for the account of their sins, kept in God’s sight and constant remembrance, with the punishment for them determined and written in the book of his decrees. Charles Ellicott names the figure: it is the great register, the book of God’s remembrance, in which men’s deeds good and evil are ever being recorded. He also presses the grammar of the next clause, which reads literally without recompensing, or except I recompense—men had taken the long-suffering of God as though it indicated forgetfulness, and they are told that he will at last requite the impenitent into their very bosom, their inmost self, for all the evil they have done. Adam Clarke says the sin is registered in heaven and calls aloud for the punishment due to it, and explains the idiom of the bosom from custom: in the East the bosom is where the pocket is, not the skirt as in the West, since the loose flowing garments have scarcely anything answering to a skirt. John Wesley supplies the human comparison—they may think God takes no notice of these things, but he will as certainly remember them as great men remember what they have recorded in writing because they would not forget it.

The second verse joins the generations. Gill reads it of the punishment of the fathers and the children alike, the sins being the same and continued from father to son, approved and committed by one generation after another until the measure was filled up, when the recompense for all of them is given at once. Wesley says the same from the other side: they are punished not only for their personal sins but for the sins of their parents, which they had made their own by imitation, and not only for late sins but for the earlier sins of the same kind that they had continued in. On the incense burnt upon the mountains, Ellicott identifies the old inveterate sin of the worship of high places, and observes that worship paid there to other gods, or paid nominally to Jehovah in a way he had forbidden, was practically a blasphemy against him; Gill says the same, that God interpreted such offerings as a reproaching of himself. Clarke contributes a textual note, preferring with the Greek version to read their iniquities and the iniquities of their fathers rather than your. Ellicott renders the closing clause I will measure their work first into their bosoms, and calls that, as it were, the primary duty of the Supreme Ruler. Keil and Delitzsch take hold of the same word and find in it the hinge of the chapter: the little adverb first of all has clearly intimated that the work of the future will not all consist in the execution of penal justice, so that there is no abruptness in the transition from threatening to promises which follows immediately.
8:
The turn to mercy comes through a vintage image. John Gill reads it as comfort: lest the truly godly should be distressed by such denunciations, a remnant according to the election of grace is to be saved from the general ruin, as when men are about to cut down a vine and a single cluster with new wine in it is seen. Matthew Henry makes the same point through Paul’s question whether God has cast away his people, and draws the picture out: when a vine is so blasted that the dresser is inclined to pluck it up, yet if ever so little juice fit for new wine is found, though but in one cluster, a stander-by interposes and says destroy it not, for there is life in the root. Good men, he adds, are blessings to the places where they live, and God sometimes spares whole cities for a few such—an honour we should be ambitious of, not only to be distinguished from others but serviceable to them. John Wesley hears a gracious answer to a prophet pleading the covenant with the patriarchs: God intended no such severity, and the threatening holds against the generality but not against all.

Charles Ellicott notes the abruptness of the transition, which suggests an interval of time, though the link may lie in the word first of his amended rendering—God chastens, but does not destroy. As one fruitful cluster leads a vine-dresser to spare an otherwise fruitless vine, so the sinful nation is spared for the twenty or the ten righteous in it. He adds a literary observation: the words destroy it not stand at the head of three Psalms as the tune to which they were sung, from which he infers a popular vintage song, apt for the prophet’s purpose. Adam Clarke reports a rabbinic reading that presses the figure further: as the cluster contains bark and kernels besides the juice, so Israel has sinners besides the just, and is not destroyed because there are righteous in it; but as bark and kernels are thrown away when the wine is pressed out, so shall the sinners be purged from among the just. He notes too that a manuscript points the next phrase in the singular, for the sake of my servant, which he refers to the Messiah and finds supported by the Greek.

The promise is then given place and people. Gill records that most understood the seed brought out of Jacob of Christ, who came of the tribe of Judah and may be signified by the cluster in which the blessing was, though others understood the apostles and the first believers. Ellicott takes Jacob and Judah for the remnants of the two kingdoms carried into captivity, and calls my mountains one of the prophet’s characteristic phrases, since not Zion only but every hill shared a derived sanctity; Clarke prefers the singular, with the Greek and Syriac, so that Zion alone is meant, as the feminine pronoun following suggests. Keil and Delitzsch read the two names that follow as marking the whole country from west to east: Sharon is the plain of rich pasture along the coast from Joppa towards Carmel, and the valley of Achor, made famous by the stoning of Achan, runs through the hills into the plain of Jericho, so that between them the wealth in flocks will extend and the same peace prevail. Henry concludes that they shall recover the whole land, have wherewith to stock it, and enjoy it with none to disturb them; Ellicott calls the district a garden of the Lord for the restored remnant. Henry describes who these are: such as serve God and such as seek him, making it the end of their lives to glorify him and the business of their lives to call upon him—and God’s faithful servants, however they are looked upon, are the best friends their country has.
11:
The address turns back on the unfaithful, and two obscure names dominate it. John Gill says the Lord here returns to the body of the people who forsook his worship, some having professed to be disciples and then walked no more with him. John Wesley explains that to forget the holy mountain signifies not regarding the true worship of God, takes the first name for the idols of the ten tribes and the Assyrians, a troop where the God of Israel was one, and the second for the multitude of their idols; the table he understands of feasts made upon their sacrifices in imitation of what God had commanded. Charles Ellicott presses the names for evidence of date. The phrase implies abandonment of the temple worship for a heathen ritual, and what follows points to Canaanite rather than Babylonian idolatry, favouring the earlier date. He takes the first as the Gad, probably the planet Jupiter, worshipped as the greater fortune, and cites the place-name Baal-Gad as evidence of how early the worship prevailed in Syria; the table he identifies with the spread feast prominent in Assyrian polytheism. The second name he takes for a Syrian deity, probably the planet Venus as the lesser fortune.

Adam Clarke is content to leave it dark. The disquisitions of the learned are infinite and uncertain, he says; the likeliest guess is that one means good fortune and the other the moon, but he quotes a scholar who asks why we should be solicitous: they were plainly false gods, either stars or a mere fiction, and the Scriptures chose rather that the memory of them be utterly abolished—and God be praised, they are so abolished that we are quite at a loss to know what they were. He does report the practice from an early description: in many cities it was an ancient custom on the last day of the year to set out a table of viands and a goblet of mixed wine, in augury of the coming year’s fertility, and the people did the same, pouring libations not on an altar but on such tables. Keil and Delitzsch trace the second name into other languages, and render the clause as filling up mixed drink for the goddess of destiny, so that what follows answers it exactly: I have destined you to the sword.

That answer is the point of the next verse. Gill notes the elegance of the expression, which plays on the name meaning number: since they furnished a drink offering to Number and trusted in it, God would number them to the sword, that none should escape. Matthew Henry draws two properties out of the threat. God’s judgments come regularly, executed according to commission, so that those fall by the sword who are counted out to it and none besides; though the sword seems to devour promiscuously, it is made to know its number. And they come irresistibly, since the stout-hearted shall be forced to bow, for none ever hardened their hearts against God and prospered. On the sins he is equally exact: idolatry was the ancient sin, and those who thought one God too little never thought scores sufficient, but were still adding to the number, pinching their families rather than stinting their devotions—which, he says, should shame the worshippers of the true God out of their niggardliness. Unbelief was the later sin, and its aggravation is that the evil was done before God’s eyes, not by surprise or inadvertency but with deliberation, and that they chose what he utterly detested. Wesley reads the bowing down as answering their bowing down to idols. Keil and Delitzsch see the renewed sentence as introducing the five contrasted pairs that follow. Clarke ends with a rabbinic saying that fits the case: turn to God one day before you die—and since no man knows that day, it is necessary to turn today.
13:
The five contrasts are read as punishment shaped to fit the sin. John Gill simply notes that the contrast is drawn between those who believed and those who rejected. Charles Ellicott makes the correspondence exact: the offence had been the orgy of an idol’s feast, so the penalty is hunger and thirst, while joy and gladness fall to those who abstained from it; and he finds a striking parallelism between these clauses and the blessings and woes of the gospel. Adam Clarke illustrates the same division with a rabbinic parable. A king invited his servants but appointed no hour for the feast. The prudent among them adorned themselves and waited at the gate of the king’s house, asking whether anything were lacking within, that is, whether there were work to be done; the foolish went off mocking, and asked when the feast would be at which there was no labour. Suddenly the king sought out his servants, and both those who were adorned and those still polluted came in; he was glad when he met the prudent and angry when he met the foolish, and gave sentence: let these sit down and eat, and let those stand and look on. Clarke observes how like the story is to the parables of the wise and foolish virgins and of the marriage of the king’s son. Of the joy on the other side Gill says it is the joy of electing, redeeming and calling grace, the heart filled with a sense of the great things God has done.

The name is the second theme. Gill takes the threat to mean the name will be left execrable to those who come after. Ellicott sets it beside other places where a name becomes a formula of cursing, and states the thought behind them: the person named is under so heavy a penalty from the wrath of God that he becomes a representative instance of what that wrath can accomplish; and precisely because the old name has been identified with evil, God will call his chosen ones, the true Israel, by another name, which shall be for blessing and not for cursing. John Wesley says the same from both ends—their names will be used as examples of the eminent wrath of God upon sinners, and God will not suffer his own people to be called by a name that idolaters are known by. Clarke adds a textual note, that the Greek and the Chaldee read the verb in the plural, shall slay you. On the last verse Gill describes the man who blesses himself as one who is sensible that he stands in need of blessings and prays for them, or who takes notice that he has them and is thankful. Ellicott renders the divine title literally as the God of the Amen, traces its echoes in the New Testament, and suggests that the prophet had entered into the inner meaning of what was to most men only a liturgical formula; the clause added about the former troubles emphasises that it is the truth and faithfulness of God, who keeps his promise for ever, that will lead men to use that new name as a benediction. Wesley puts the ground of it plainly: they shall bless by the God of truth because they shall see what he promised fulfilled, and the former troubles are hidden because they are at an end.
17:
How literally to take the new creation divides the voices. Adam Clarke lays out the range: some take it literally, that God will change the atmosphere and make the earth more fruitful; some refer it to the millennium, others to a glorious state of religion, others to the re-creation of the earth after fire. His own judgment is that it points primarily to the deliverance from the captivity and ultimately to the conversion of the Jews. John Gill holds that the prophecy began to be accomplished in the first times of the Gospel, when a new face of things appeared and the whole looked like a new world—a new church state gathered out of the world, new ordinances, a more spiritual worship—and will be further accomplished at the conversion of the Jews, which will be as life from the dead. John Wesley reads it of a wholesale change in the state not only of God’s people but of the world, so glorious that the former will not be remembered. Charles Ellicott traces the thought through the New Testament, where it recurs verbally and again in the restitution of all things, and says the former things, the sin and sorrow of the past, will fade from the memory of God’s people, absorbed in everlasting joy.

Matthew Henry allows the earlier fulfilment—the promises were in part made good when the people were settled again in their own land as in a new world—but says they have full accomplishment in the gospel church, militant and at length triumphant, so that in the graces believers have from Christ we are to look for this new heaven and new earth. He marks how the promise rises: the previous verse said the former troubles were forgotten, but here even the former world is forgotten, and those converted were so transported with the comforts of the faith that everything known before became as nothing—not their foregoing griefs only, but their foregoing joys, were swallowed up. Two things follow. The divine power is inexhaustible, since the God who created one heaven and earth can create another; and the happiness of the saints is entire, for when God is reconciled to us, giving us a new heaven, the creatures too are reconciled to us, giving us a new earth.

The joy that follows is described from several sides. Gill takes what is created to be either the persons converted, new creatures with new principles of life wrought in them, every such instance being matter of joy to angels and saints and especially to ministers, or else the whole state of things under the Gospel, itself a new world of God’s creating. Clarke renders the summons an exultation in the age to come. Ellicott observes that from the prophet’s standpoint the earthly city, transformed and transfigured, holds the central place in the new creation, and that in the New Testament the promise is transferred to the Jerusalem which is above. Henry orders the joys: all who belong to the church shall rejoice, and she shall not only rejoice but be rejoiced in; her prosperity shall be a rejoicing to God himself, who in all their affliction was afflicted, so that he will not only rejoice in her well-doing but rejoice to do her good and rest in his love—and what God rejoices in, it becomes us to rejoice in. Gill says the same of the divine joy, looking for its accomplishment when the tabernacle of God shall be with men. On the silencing of weeping Henry distinguishes: if it relates to the church in this life it means only that the former occasions of grief shall not return, but in heaven it will be fulfilled in both the perfection and the perpetuity of the joy, where all tears shall be wiped away. Clarke reports a rabbinic gloss tying the promise to the next verse: weeping ceases because untimely death ceases.
20:
The promised life is long rather than endless, and the voices are careful about the difference. John Gill reads the first clause of burial: there shall no more be carried out from the city an infant that has lived but a few days, a very common thing now, whereas in the latter day such instances will be rare or none at all, every child born living to the age of a man and not cut off by premature death, whether by disease or famine or sword. Charles Ellicott states the limit plainly: the prophet sees in the restored city not so much an eternal and deathless life as the return of the traditional longevity of the antediluvian and patriarchal age, life no longer cut short by pestilence and war, so that a man dying at a hundred will be thought of as dying young, and even the sinner, dying before his time as the penalty of his guilt, will live out the measure of a century. What he finds most noticeable is that sin is here thought of as not altogether extinct, still appearing, though under altered conditions, even in the restored city. John Wesley makes the same double point: those who are now children shall die at a great age, yet none of this shall be of any advantage to wicked men, who if they live to a hundred shall die accursed. Adam Clarke contributes only a textual note, that three of the ancient versions read there rather than thence.

The two verses that follow reverse a curse. Keil and Delitzsch point out that where the law had threatened building without inhabiting and planting without eating, the very opposite here receives its fullest realisation: they themselves will enjoy what they have worked for, without anyone else stepping in to take possession of what they have built and planted, whether a countryman by violence or by inheritance or a foreigner by plunder or conquest; and the duration of their life will be as great as that of trees, of the oaks and terebinths and cedars that live for ages. Ellicott calls the picture the proverbial type of national security and peace, as its opposite was of national misfortune, and adds a literary observation on the comparison: poets have commonly likened the lives of men to the leaves of deciduous trees, whereas here they are likened to the life of the tree itself—and he insists that the prophet is still speaking not of national but of individual life, with the cedars of Lebanon or the oaks of Bashan supplying the ideal standard. Gill points the reversal at a particular memory, that the Israelites had once inhabited houses the Canaanites built, whereas these shall inhabit the houses they build themselves and not be dispossessed by an enemy. Clarke takes the measure of the figure literally and canvasses what it is worth: the oak is commonly supposed to last about a thousand years, five hundred growing to full perfection and as many decaying, which he thinks a moderate and probable computation; he reports far larger claims made for certain eastern trees, one said to be still only in its prime after an enormous age, though he suspects those figures of being enlarged; and he notes the rabbinic application of the phrase to the tree of life. His own conclusion is the same as Ellicott’s, that the prophet means his people shall live to the age of those before the flood.
23:
Labour that comes to nothing is removed first. John Gill spells out what it reverses: men build houses and enemies turn them out, or plant vineyards and strangers devour them, or the crop is smitten with blasting and mildew. Adam Clarke moves the phrase my chosen from the end of the previous verse to the beginning of this, on the authority of three ancient versions and against the received division, and calls the Greek rendering beautiful: my chosen shall not labour in vain, neither beget children for the curse. On the next clause he prefers the sense that they shall not generate a short-lived race, supporting it from a psalm where the same word describes days consumed in vanity. Charles Ellicott reads it as a picture of a patriarchal family of many generations together, fathers no longer outliving their children and mourning for them as the patriarch did, and as men had done in the times of war and famine through which the prophet lived.

The answer that outruns the prayer follows. Keil and Delitzsch put it as a matter of wills brought into agreement: the will of the church of the new Jerusalem will be so perfectly the will of God that he will hear the slightest emotion of prayer in the heart, the half-uttered petition, and at once fulfil it. Ellicott states it by contrast with present experience, where there is commonly an interval between prayer and answer, whereas here the two would be simultaneous, or the answer anticipate the prayer. John Wesley notes that God had promised earlier to answer when they called, and promises here to answer the words as soon as they are formed in the heart, before they can get them out of their lips. Gill gives it a setting: should they be attacked, or fear disturbance, and bethink themselves of applying to the Lord, before they can put up one petition in a regular way he will appear for them and give an answer of peace.

The closing picture of peace among the animals is handled at three levels. Keil and Delitzsch treat it first as a literary fact: the prophet repeats an earlier passage of his own almost word for word, in a compendious abridgment, and while such self-repetition favours unity of authorship, one word used here occurs elsewhere only in the latest books, which might be adduced on the other side. The one new thing in the picture, they add, is what is said of the serpent. Ellicott takes the verse for what have been called the discords in the harmony of nature, the pain and death involved of necessity in the relation of one class of animals to another; in the new heaven and new earth there would be no such discords, the flesh-eating beasts changing their nature, and the serpent, named probably as the starting-point of those discords, finding food in the dust it crawls in and destroying no longer, so that the ideal Paradise is restored. He notes a close parallel in a Roman poet and leaves open whether poet and prophet stand on the same footing, and whether a literal fulfilment is to be looked for. Gill and Wesley read the animals as men. Gill makes the people of God the lambs, for harmlessness, and wicked men the wolves, for fierceness, and says that by grace the latter become as gentle as the former and feed with them on the same spiritual food, persecutors of the church becoming members of it, as in the first times of the Gospel; Wesley has God taking off the fierceness of his people’s enemies, and reads the serpent eating dust, its proper meat, instead of flying upon men, as a promise that the wicked shall no more devour the people of God. Clarke draws one boundary: the salvation procured is for men, and fallen spirits abide under the curse still.
